summary:
MARS NAV is an interactive scientific mission-planning platform designed to transform NASA's Mars exploration data into practical decision-support tools.

Our team developed a regional exploration system for Jezero Crater using NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX elevation models and orbital imagery, combined with USGS geological maps.

Users can explore Martian terrain in 2D and 3D, identify geological formations, select scientific destinations, and compare three routes using A* pathfinding and terrain-slope analysis. The platform also includes multi-stop mission planning, elevation profiles, assisted waypoint selection, and conceptual rover and resource estimations.

Our regional dataset covers approximately 89 × 101 km, with route calculations performed on a grid of approximately 100 meters per cell.

MARS NAV connects geological discovery with terrain-aware route planning in one accessible experience. It demonstrates how open planetary data can support scientific exploration, engineering education, and early-stage mission analysis.

The platform is a research and educational prototype, not a certified navigation system.
details:
MARS NAV — From Martian Data to Scientific Decisions

1. The Problem

Exploring Mars requires more than identifying destinations on a map. Mission planners must understand terrain elevation, avoid challenging slopes, identify scientifically valuable locations, and consider the resources needed to complete an exploration.

NASA provides extensive planetary datasets, but combining them into an accessible planning environment can be challenging, especially for students and emerging researchers.

Our team, THE BOYS6, developed MARS NAV to address this challenge.

2. Our Solution

MARS NAV is an interactive scientific mission-planning prototype focused on Jezero Crater, Mars.

It combines NASA orbital imagery, digital elevation models, and USGS geological mapping to help users explore terrain, compare alternative routes, and design scientific expeditions.

Users can:

  • Explore Martian terrain using interactive 2D maps and 3D terrain visualization.
  • Identify geological formations and investigate their scientific significance.
  • Select a starting point, intermediate scientific stops, and a destination.
  • Compare three routes generated through A* pathfinding.
  • Analyze distances, elevation changes, terrain slopes, and topographic risk categories.
  • Receive assisted waypoint suggestions when a selected location is restricted by the terrain model.
  • Compare conceptual exploration platforms and estimate mission resources.
  • Export mission reports containing route statistics and planning assumptions.

3. How It Works

Step 1 — Processing NASA Data

We use digital elevation models and orbital imagery acquired by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, particularly data from its Context Camera (CTX) and High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE).

The regional CTX dataset covers approximately 89 × 101 kilometers, with a native DEM resolution of 20 meters per pixel and an orbital image resolution of approximately 5 meters per pixel.

For regional route planning, terrain data is processed into a grid of approximately 100 meters per cell to make computational analysis manageable.

Step 2 — Terrain Risk Analysis

The system calculates terrain slopes from elevation data and classifies them into four categories:

  • Low slope: 0–5°.
  • Moderate slope: 5–10°.
  • High slope: 10–15°.
  • Restricted: above 15°.

These thresholds are exploratory planning assumptions, not NASA-certified mobility limits.

Step 3 — Route Optimization

Our routing engine uses the A* search algorithm to generate three alternatives: shortest, balanced, and conservative.

Each alternative applies a different weighting between travel distance and terrain-slope penalties.

Users can introduce intermediate stops and compare routes using distance, cumulative ascent, descent, and slope exposure.

Step 4 — Geological Exploration

MARS NAV integrates the USGS Geologic Map of Jezero Crater and Nili Planum (Scientific Investigations Map 3464).

Users can select geological polygons, inspect unit names and codes, and associate scientific destinations with mapped geological information.

Step 5 — Mission Resource Planning

The application includes conceptual rover profiles, equipment selections, energy budgets, travel-time estimates, and simplified mission-resource calculations.

These models allow users to explore planning trade-offs. They are not validated specifications of actual NASA rovers.

4. Technologies and Tools

Our project combines scientific geospatial processing, backend development, and interactive visualization.

Programming languages: Python and JavaScript.

Backend: FastAPI, NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, GeoPandas, Shapely, and A* pathfinding.

Frontend: React, Vite, OpenLayers, Three.js, HTML, and CSS.

Development tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub, and Windows PowerShell.

Scientific data sources:

  • NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter — CTX imagery and elevation products.
  • NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter — HiRISE terrain data.
  • United States Geological Survey — Geologic Map of Jezero Crater and Nili Planum (SIM 3464).

The current prototype is a web-based software application and does not require specialized physical hardware.

5. Innovation and Creativity

MARS NAV goes beyond displaying planetary imagery.

Its main innovation is connecting three stages of scientific exploration in one workflow:

Identify a scientific destination → Compare terrain-aware routes → Evaluate mission resources.

The system brings geological information, pathfinding, visualization, and conceptual operational planning into a common interface.

The regional-to-local approach also demonstrates how different NASA datasets can support different planning scales.

Rather than treating every map as equally precise, MARS NAV distinguishes regional planning from higher-resolution local terrain analysis.

6. Benefits and Potential Impact

MARS NAV can help students, educators, researchers, and engineering teams understand how planetary data contributes to mission planning.

Its benefits include:

  • Making complex NASA planetary datasets easier to explore.
  • Connecting geological interpretation with computational route planning.
  • Supporting education in robotics, aerospace engineering, geospatial analysis, and planetary science.
  • Encouraging transparent, data-driven mission decisions.
  • Providing a foundation for future research into multi-resolution navigation and robotic exploration.

7. Scientific Limitations and Future Development

MARS NAV is an educational and research prototype, not a certified navigation system for operational Mars missions.

Its regional routing grid cannot identify every rock, narrow obstacle, sand hazard, or mobility constraint. Its rover performance and resource models use configurable assumptions rather than validated flight-system parameters.

Future work could include higher-resolution route refinement, terrain traversability models, verified rover specifications, additional NASA imagery, and automated scientific-target prioritization.

8. Our Vision

Our goal is to transform open planetary information into an accessible tool that helps people understand not only where to explore Mars, but also why a destination matters and how an expedition could be planned.

MARS NAV turns planetary maps into scientific mission-planning experiences.
